newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends near flat vs mark, lower vs yen in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends near flat vs mark, lower vs yen in U.S..

text.p: The dollar held steady in U.S. trade against the mark after a sharp sell-off just before the open, but continued its march lower against the yen on Thursday as U.S. stocks tumbled, dealers said.

"The dollar's drop is a combination of profit-taking along with uncertainty about the future," said Hans Boman, chief spot dealer at Swedbank in New York, pointing to a fall of almost 100 points in the Dow Jones Industrials stock average on Thursday.
"It's difficult to tell what is going to happen from here and the dollar's flying up and down," he added.

The dollar fell sharply to open markedly lower in the U.S. from it's previous close against the mark after signs of economic strength in Europe and more verbal attempts by the Bundesbank chief to tame the dollar's recent strength.
Robust results from an index which tracks the West German business climate and solid German money supply growth in January bolstered the mark at the dollar's expense.
The Ifo index rose to 93.3 in January from December's 90.0 while Germany's M3 money supply grew an annualized 11.7 percent in January versus the fourth quarter of 1996.

"The German M3 money supply and Ifo survey were stronger than expected and that has diminished any real potential for an imminent rate cut in Germany," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd in Chicago.

The dollar fell to its lowest level since February 10 against the yen, closing at 122.50/60 yen, two yen below Wednesday's 124.50/60 close. Dollar/yen opened in the U.S. at 122.95/00. Against the mark, the dollar ended at 1.6860/65, a whisker higher than its opening rate of 1.6840/50, but significantly lower than Wednesday's 1.6975/85 close.

The dollar was also hit by another call from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer for an end to the dollar's rise against the mark. Tietmeyer voiced similar cries a number of times earlier this week, dealers said.

Tietmeyer said, in a previously taped interview for Hungarian radio, that the dollar's recent gains were a correction, "but we are not interested in a correction process that would go beyond tolerable limits". Tietmeyer added that a German interest rate cut was not likely in the short run.

The dollar also fell victim to a surge in the mark against the Norwegian crown after Norway's central bank surprised the markets by announcing it would resume foreign currency purchases. On January 10, the bank had said it would curb intervention in the currency market.

Norway's central bank stressed it will resume foreign currency purchases, but not "as exchange market interventions", a subtle distinction which led to market confusion immediately following the announcement.
The mark also benefitted from a sharp drop in British pound following news the Confederation of British Industry had cut its economic growth forecast, citing the pound's strength.

Meanwhile, the Japanese yen strengthened on speculation, later denied by a Ministry of Finance official, that the Japanese government was considering allocating new public funds to buy collateralized land formerly owned by troubled financial firms. The prospect of future monetary aid to Japan's troubled banking sector helped the yen, dealers said.
Also hurting the dollar against the yen was the movement of key short-term interest rates in Japan.
The Japanese call rate rose above the nation's discount rate, an unusual relationship which suggests there is some room for the dollar to fall against the yen, analysts said.

The dollar received a brief lift after a strong reading in the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia index of business conditions. The index climbed to 17.4 in February, beating expectations for a 10.0 reading and January's 11.3 showing.

The dollar rose to 1.4765/70 Swiss francs from 1.4752/62, and Canadian $1.3620/25 from $1.3569/74. Sterling rose to $1.6120/30 from $1.6095/05. The Australian dollar rose to $0.7735/40 from $0.7680/85.
